To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

plasmonic Au nanorods can exhibit a fourth-order photoemission when deposited on Pt substrates, and that Au nanorods deposited on ITO exhibit third-order photoemissions, with a plasmon resonance frequency almost identical to that in solution, but with a substantial change in work function.

the plasmon resonance frequency of single Au nanorod arrays on indium tin oxide films is almost unshiftedd compared to aqueous solutions, whereas Au nanorods supported on 2 nm thin Pt films exhibit strongly redshifted resonances, and that Au nanorods deposited on ITO exhibit third-order multiphoton photoionization, which is absent in both ITO films and bare Au particles.

plasmon-mediated photoemission from Au nanorods is observed only in a thin Pt film support, while Au nanorods deposited on ITO substrates exhibit a strong plasmon resonance but no plasmon-mediated multiphoton photoemission.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a scanning photoionization microscope for the investigation of ultrafast plasmonic phenomena.
the development of a novel ultrafast scanning photoionization microscope (SPIM) for the investigation of plasmon-mediated photoemission from single metal nanoparticles.
the study of plasmon-mediated photoemission processes in single Au nanospheres and Au nanorods deposited on Pt and ITO substrates.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Au nanorodes exhibit fourth-order photoemission on a thin metal substrate and a third-order photoemisson on a thin dielectric substrate.
plasmon-enhancement is only observed in the presence of an appropriate substrate, which in this case would be the ITO substrate.
plasmon-enhancement of photoemission is a complex process, involving both electrostatic and electromagnetic particle-substrate interactions.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
plasmon resonant SPIM of single metal nanostructures is feasible only if plasmon-substrate coupling is weak.
the photoemission properties of single Au nanorod on Pt are governed by plasmon-substrate interactions, whereas those for Au nanorod/ITO are dominated by electrostatic interactions.
we have developed a technique that allows the study of the plasmon resonance of single metal nanoparticles under vacuum conditions.
The main takeaway from our work is that
SPIM can be used to investigate fundamental interactions between plasmonic particles and substrates, with the potential to elucidate the mechanisms behind plasmon-mediated photoemission.
plasmonic nanostructures are highly sensitive probes of their local environment, and that this sensitivity can be exploited in SPIM to probe fundamental properties of the substrate.
the SPIM technique provides an ideal tool for studying plasmon-mediated multiphoton photoionization processes at the single particle level.
